draft.title: The Bill of Rights
card: Many people feared the new national government could threaten freedoms, as Britain's rule had. Some states hesitated to accept the Constitution without protections.
To answer this, Congress proposed amendments (formal changes to the Constitution). The first ten, adopted in 1791, are called the Bill of Rights.
They protect rights such as freedom of speech, freedom of religion and a fair trial by jury. They limit what the national government can do to people.
The Bill of Rights was added after the Constitution was written, as a written guard against government overreach.
draft.remember: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, added to guard individual freedoms from the national government.

a.q: Why was the Bill of Rights added to the Constitution?
opts: To protect freedoms from the national government
To give the national government new powers over states
To set up the three branches of the national government
To bring the war with Britain to a formal end
a.why: People worried a strong national government might threaten freedoms, so written protections were added. The three branches were already in the original Constitution, so they were not the reason.
a.clue: Think about what people feared from a strong national government.

b.q: A town bans a newspaper from printing criticism of the national government. Which protection in the Bill of Rights does this go against?
opts: Freedom of speech
Trial by jury
Freedom of religion
The power to tax
b.why: Printing criticism is a form of free expression, which the Bill of Rights protects. Freedom of religion covers beliefs and worship, so it does not fit this case.
b.clue: The newspaper is expressing its views.

a.best: To protect freedoms from the national government

problems.detail: The scenario has a town, a local government, ban the newspaper. The card says the Bill of Rights limits what the national government can do. When it was adopted in 1791 it did not bind states or towns; that came only through the 14th Amendment and 20th-century court rulings. The question contradicts the card and misleads students about whom the Bill of Rights restrained. Have the national government, or Congress, pass the ban instead.
